analysis.one_liner: Sends families $3,000 per child, $3,600 for young children, as a fully refundable tax credit.
analysis.headline: The Senate referred the child-tax-credit expansion to the Finance Committee on the day it was introduced in October 2017, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would replace the existing child tax credit with a larger one: $3,000 per child age 6 or older and $3,600 for each child under 6, growing each year with inflation. Unlike the credit at the time, it would be fully refundable, meaning families who owe little or no income tax would still get the full amount, and it would set up monthly payments from the Treasury instead of one lump sum at tax time. The credit would phase down for single parents earning above $75,000 and couples above $110,000. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with children, and especially low- and moderate-income families. Making the credit fully refundable means the poorest families — those who owe little or no federal income tax — would receive the full $3,000 or $3,600 per child in cash, rather than being limited by what they owe. Monthly advance payments would spread the money through the year instead of waiting for tax season.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families with children, especially low-income ones

how_it_helps.text: Replaces the existing child tax credit with $3,000 per child age 6 or older and $3,600 (120 percent of that) for each child under 6.
Makes the credit fully refundable, so families with little or no income tax liability receive the full amount rather than only what they owe in tax.
Requires Treasury to set up a program for advance monthly payments of the credit, so money arrives through the year.
Increases the credit amount annually for inflation after 2017.
Phases the credit down above $75,000 of income for single filers and $110,000 for joint filers, so the benefit is aimed at lower- and middle-income families.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally, because the bill contains no offsetting tax increases or spending cuts — the cost of larger, fully refundable credits would add to the deficit. Households earning above the phase-out thresholds would see their credit reduced or eliminated.

drawbacks.text: The bill includes no offsetting revenue: expanding and fully refunding the credit is deficit-financed, leaving the cost to future taxpayers or future borrowing.
Because the credit phases down as income rises above the thresholds, families near $75,000 or $110,000 face higher effective marginal tax rates on each additional dollar earned.

Advance monthly payments are reconciled against the credit a family ultimately qualifies for; families whose income rises during the year can receive more than they are owed and must repay the excess at tax time.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is large and targeted: a bigger, fully refundable credit reaches children in the poorest families, who under the credit then on the books received little or nothing. The main cost is fiscal — the bill raises no money to pay for itself — and the phase-down thresholds create some steep benefit reductions for families just above them. Whether that trade is worth it depends on how one weighs direct child support against deficit growth.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Michael Bennet, joined by Sen. Sherrod Brown, introduced the bill on October 26, 2017.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance.
No further action appears in the record: the Finance Committee held no markup and the full Senate never voted on the bill before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Families with children received nothing from this bill. Households above the phase-out thresholds kept their tax bills unchanged, and the existing child tax credit rules remained in place for the rest of the Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wealthier households and the status quo

for.name: Michael Bennet
for.what_they_did: Introduced the American Family Act of 2017 in the Senate on October 26, 2017.

for.name: Sherrod Brown
for.what_they_did: Joined Bennet in introducing the bill as an original cosponsor.

against.name: Orrin Hatch
against.what_they_did: As committee chairman, took no action on the bill after its referral — no hearing or markup appears in the record for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 10 cosponsors were Democrats and no Senate Republican signed on; with Republicans holding the Senate majority and the Finance Committee chairmanship, the bill never advanced past referral.

industries.note: The credit phases down starting at $75,000 for single filers and $110,000 for joint filers, so families above those levels would have received reduced or no benefit. Their tax liability would have stayed unchanged, while the bill's cost fell on federal taxpayers as a whole.
